article.title: how to build a one-person company using Kimi K3
article.preview_text:
i wrote the A-Z blueprint for building an AI-native company with agents...
not another swarm of bots... a system that decides what work matters, what agents may do, and what they must leave behind.

blocks.text: i wrote the A-Z blueprint for building an AI-native company with agents...
not another swarm of bots... a system that decides what work matters, what agents may do, and what they must leave behind.
core insight: harness will determine how ai-native companies allot compute. for this experiment Kimi K3 works as the central intelligence unit which powers the entire ai-native company foundry
TLDR: If you don't want to read the 4,800 words in this article, you can just go to this https://github.com/codejunkie99/company-foundry.
a company is not a group of agents. it is the method that tells them what work matters, what they may do, and what they must leave behind.
i do not want an AI CEO.
i want work to enter once, find the right context and model, follow a known method, stay inside clear limits, and leave an artifact the next person can trust.
That is a much less dramatic idea. It is also much more useful.
the wrong starting point
Most teams build the visible AI before the company: a chat window, coding agent, research agent, tool access, and a folder of prompts. Then they call it a team.
Then the work starts to matter.
The questions become operational:
Where did this customer claim come from?
Why did this task use the most expensive model?
Who gave the worker access to a customer system?
Which instructions produced this dashboard?
Can someone repeat the result without reading the entire chat history?
What happens to company knowledge when the model changes?
The usual answer is more chat: another prompt, another bot, another dashboard, and another person who knows where the important context lives.
activity is not an organisation
That creates activity. It does not create an organisation.
→ the model is rented
→ the agent is replaceable
→ the operating method is owned
This is the project I want to build: Company Foundry.
Company Foundry takes a real company brief and compiles it into an operating method. Its first native target is DeepSeek Harness.
It creates the context, skills, routes, policies, packets, evidence records, artifacts, and operating surface as one coherent system.
prove one workflow first
The first version does not need to run an entire company. It needs to make one important workflow real.
For example: customer evidence becomes a product decision brief, with sources, named assumptions, an approved model route, and a visible artifact.
That is the starting line for an AI-native company.
the thing we are actually building
The product is not a new agent team.
It is not a prompt library with a nicer interface. It is not a control plane bolted onto DeepSeek Harness. It is not a dashboard that watches agents work.
It is a compiler for organisational method.
compile the company once
Someone describes the company once: product, customers, goals, sources, systems, permissions, budgets, rules, and current work.
The compiler turns that description into a portable company specification, then generates the files and runtime configuration a harness can use.
The universal output looks like this:
This is deliberately boring. It does not try to model every meeting, person, or feeling in a business.
It records the parts that make work reproducible: purpose, ownership, evidence, authority, output, and review.
contracts make the folder useful
For DeepSeek Harness, the compiler produces a company preset and a set of plugins:
The folder is not the product. The contracts inside it are.
One contract defines ownership, another task admission, another source policy, and another model eligibility.
The final contracts decide whether a result may leave the company and how that result is measured.
make models replaceable
This matters because every AI company will use more than one model.
Kimi K3 can handle the first build. It can turn a company brief into an initial working harness, reason over a scoped work packet, create code and artifacts, and help refine the method.
But the company should never assume that one model stays best forever. The harness owns the company method. The router selects the worker.
why an agent is not a company
An agent is good at a turn of work.
It can read a task, inspect context, call tools, make a plan, write code, research a question, or create a draft.
That is valuable. It still does not have a company purpose, budget, permission boundary, or durable record of why a decision was made.
A company has to survive the end of a session.
sessions end. companies continue.
The durable layer has four jobs:
Remember what customers said without treating generated summaries as fact.
Record whether a decision came from evidence, an inference, or a guess.
Match model cost and capability to the consequence of the task.
Stop a worker from acting externally merely because it has the tool.
A company has a method.
The method needs a stable shape:
Every arrow is a place where work can become unclear.
every arrow is a failure boundary
A vague goal makes workers optimise the wrong thing.
Uncontrolled context leaks sensitive or irrelevant information into a run.
Hand-copied skills let two workers use different methods without saying so.
A hidden route makes cost and quality impossible to explain.
An artifact without evidence turns a fluent guess into company memory.
This is what makes the word *harness* useful.

A harness is the layer that gives agent work shape. It composes the available capabilities, creates scoped context, runs work, records what happened, and exposes the same truth through different surfaces.
The company layer adds two questions above the usual agent loop:
→ can this worker do the task?
→ should the company do this work, with this evidence, under these limits, at this cost?
That question should not live inside a giant system prompt.
start with a company brief, not an agent prompt
The first input to Company Foundry is a company brief.
This is not a brand document. It is not a long founder memo. It is a structured description of what the company needs the harness to know in order to operate safely and usefully.
The smallest useful brief contains six things.
Identity. What does the company sell, who is it for, and what should a worker never assume?
Goals. Which outcomes are active now, and which ideas are merely interesting?
Evidence. Which sources are approved, reliable, current, and accessible for this work?
Authority. What may a worker observe, prepare, change, or send?
Resources. Which repos, apps, tools, models, and data stores exist, and what do they cost?
Standards. What must a finished artifact contain, and which claims or changes require review?
The company brief must remain separate from the model conversation.
Kimi K3 can turn loose company notes into a structured first pass and expose missing constraints. The result belongs in company configuration, never in one agent’s chat history.
prompt 01: compile the company before you create workers
Give Kimi K3 the raw company notes and make it expose the missing decisions:
Kimi K3 is not deciding what the company is. It is compiling what the company has actually decided.
That makes it inspectable. It also makes it replaceable.
When a customer segment changes, update the company profile.
When a source is no longer approved, update the source policy.
When model economics change, update the model registry.
The next relevant packet receives the new rule without rewriting every worker prompt.
→ prompts describe a moment
→ company records describe a method
→ a harness applies the method to the moment
the first principle: work must leave a trace
The dangerous part of agent work is not that a model can write.
The dangerous part is that it can change things outside itself.
It can create a record, open a pull request, update a dashboard, post a message, spend money, or contact a customer.
These are not merely tool calls. They are emissions from the company into the outside world.
The harness should make a hard distinction between four levels of authority.
four levels of authority
Observe: inspect approved information, documents, repositories, or dashboards.
Prepare: create a private candidate artifact, draft, branch, or dashboard definition.
Commit: change company state through a reviewed record or operation.
Emit: send information or trigger an action outside the company boundary.
Observe and prepare can be broad. Commit and emit need explicit limits.
This is not bureaucracy. It is how you make fast work reversible.
An agent should be able to explore several approaches inside an isolated scope. It should be able to produce drafts, candidate code, and retries without creating permanent debris.
But the company needs a clear point where the work becomes real.
Before an external effect, the system stores its target, intended change, evidence, actor, approval rule, and compensation path. The effect stays proposed until the gate clears it.
the effect becomes real at the gate
An email can be drafted many times. Sending it is one event.
A pull request can be prepared many times. Merging it is one event.
A research brief can be rewritten many times. Using it to change the product roadmap is one decision.
This gives the company a simple safety rule:
→ explore freely inside the work scope
→ commit deliberately to company state
→ emit externally only through a visible gate
The model does not decide its own authority. The work packet and policy do. That is what turns a tool-using agent into automation the company can trust.
DeepSeek Harness is where the company becomes executable
DeepSeek Harness is a good first native target because it is designed around composition.
Models, tools, persistence, policy, interfaces, and agent behavior are separate capabilities.
Each capability has a stable definition, a provider, and named consumers. That makes the system flexible without making it vague.
DeepSeek Harness hands the company four rules worth copying:
A capability is a declared service with a stable contract.
A provider implements it while consumers depend on the contract.
A gate blocks admission until required services exist, while a lock orders withdrawal and cleanup.
A state mutation returns its inverse so the change can be rolled back and traced.
Company Foundry should add company capabilities in the same way.
company-profile resolves identity, rules, source policy, and scoped context.
company-router selects an eligible model and records why it was chosen.
company-skills loads a versioned method with its templates, tools, and checks.
company-evidence records sources, extracts, claims, confidence, and review state.
company-artifacts creates durable outputs with provenance.
company-dashboard projects packets, approvals, routes, costs, artifacts, and failures.
prompt 02: turn the company contract into DeepSeek Harness capabilities
The second prompt crosses the boundary from organisational design into executable infrastructure:
This is the point where a prompt becomes engineering work. The output must contain seams, failure behavior, and tests, not a picture of an architecture.
The key is that these are capabilities, not special instructions for one role.
The capability boundary changes three things:
Customer research becomes a service any approved workflow can use.
Model routing becomes policy applied before work begins.
Every artifact receives a path, type, owner, inputs, status, and review record.
one packet gets one boundary
The harness also creates a useful boundary around a session.
One work packet gets only the skills, sources, tools, route, and permissions it needs. A research task does not receive deployment access. A coding task does not receive customer data by default.
The task remains resumable because its model-visible context and meaningful events are recorded with the run.
The user interface is only one surface on that system.
Every surface should show the same company truth, whether it is a command line, dashboard, review queue, or app.
customer research is the first real company skill
The most useful early workflow is customer research.

It connects directly to product, sales, support, and strategy. It is easy to make impressive-looking but unreliable. It forces the company to define sources, evidence, claims, review, artifacts, and decision boundaries.
That makes it the right test.
Do not start with the request “research our customers.” Start with a work packet:
Now the work has a shape.
prompt 03: run research as a bounded swarm
One model can execute the packet sequentially. A swarm can split it without splitting the truth.
The collectors run in parallel because they share a schema, not a memory.
The synthesizer receives the ledger instead of four conversations. The reviewer receives the claims and evidence instead of the other workers’ confidence.
A swarm is a temporary execution shape. It is not the organisation chart.
the ledger is the shared memory
Discover: list the segments, unknowns, product terms, competitors, and evidence gaps.
Collect: record each source with an ID, type, location, date, access state, and excerpts.
Synthesize: separate what the company knows, infers, and still needs to learn.
Review: reject unsupported claims, scope leaks, and recommendations that outrun the evidence.

The finished artifact should contain more than polished prose. It should contain a source ledger, a claim table, open questions, recommended next actions, the skill version, the route record, and the review status.
That artifact can then become input to a product skill.
The product skill consumes the approved brief instead of researching the question again. It can create a problem map, identify product bets, prepare a specification, and record the decision.
A coding skill can then consume the approved specification and prepare an isolated implementation plan or pull request.
This is how the company accumulates a method rather than a pile of generated documents.
skills are not prompts. they are company methods.
A skill file is useful. It is not enough.
A company skill needs an identity, a version, an owner, an allowed scope, required inputs, expected artifacts, authority boundaries, tools, source rules, and an evaluation.
For a customer-research skill, the contract might say:
This is much more portable than a giant role prompt.

The same skill can run through Kimi K3 today, another model tomorrow, or a different agent runtime later. The underlying instructions may change because models behave differently. The company contract stays stable.
the registry makes the method operable
Skills should live in a registry, not in a random folder.
The registry answers which version created an artifact, which skills can use sensitive data, and which methods can create a pull request.
It also shows who owns each output, which artifacts depend on a changed skill, and which evaluation is failing.
There are two useful families in the first registry.
Company skills produce insight briefs, account plans, decision memos, market maps, operating reviews, and dashboards.
Build skills produce code plans, repository maps, pull requests, tests, app prototypes, design implementations, and release notes.
Both families follow the same contract. The difference is the capability they require and the authority they may receive.
prompt 04: write the skill registry and the skill files together
Do not ask Kimi K3 for a list of clever agent roles. Ask for executable methods:

Company Foundry can compile these definitions into native skill files and presets. Kimi K3 can help author them. DeepSeek Harness can load and run them. The registry remains the company’s source of truth.
This is where Kimi K3 is valuable in the first build. It can create a code skill, inspect a repository, produce a scoped implementation plan, and generate an artifact inside the harness.
But it should run under a defined packet with a named scope, route record, and evaluation. It should never receive “improve the product” plus a collection of production credentials.
The output of a good skill is not just text. It is a repeatable work method with a visible result.
route models like a company spends money
A model picker is for a person.
A model router is for a company.

The router receives task requirements before the run starts. It knows whether the task needs low cost, low latency, large context, tool use, computer use, structured output, code generation, or high-quality synthesis.
It filters out ineligible models, then chooses from the remaining routes according to company policy.
The first policy can be small:
prompt 05: make the router earn every expensive call
The router should be designed against real packets before it is trusted with live work:
In a swarm, this decision happens per worker. Extraction can use an economy route while synthesis uses a capable route. Parallel work should not multiply premium-model spend by accident.
Kimi K3 can sit in the capable tier where its quality is useful. That is not a permanent claim about every task.
The router should use company evaluations, cost, availability, and task requirements to choose the route.
the receipt is the debugging surface
Every route needs a receipt:
The company can now answer why a cost occurred before the invoice arrives.
It can also learn. If the output was weak, inspect the packet, source set, skill version, selected route, model result, and evaluation. Do not reduce the diagnosis to “AI was wrong.”
The router owns trade-offs. The agent owns the task.
That division prevents a common failure: every agent asks for the strongest model because the agent has no reason to care about cost, latency, or company-wide capacity.
the Company Room is the proof
The first user experience should be a Company Room, not a fantasy dashboard with animated agents.
A working room where a person can ask one important company question and see the system turn it into accountable work.
For example:
The room should expose the whole run:
packet, owner, context, and source set
skill version, model route, and authority level
work log, evidence, artifact, cost, and pending approval
This makes the harness legible.
the room reads records, not reasoning
A leader can see whether the system is producing useful work.
An operator can see why a run is waiting.
A reviewer can inspect the artifact and its evidence.
An engineer can trace the dashboard to the skill, route, and inputs.
The room borrows a normalised event stream so different providers can expose work without leaking their private formats into the interface.
It also borrows a permission broker with a strict default: when the permission service is unavailable, the risky action stops.
The rule is simple: a pending ask resolves to deny when the broker disappears. With no answerer, the caller does not guess. The caller stops.
The Company Room should borrow the pattern, not the product shape.
The core is responsibilities, packets, authority, artifacts, evidence, and evaluations. Workers bind to roles for a task, runtimes execute it, and the company record keeps the durable method.
prompt 06: generate the dashboard from the run record
This is where Kimi K3 can turn the same contracts into a usable app artifact:
The prompt forces the interface to reveal the work without becoming a second source of truth.
The interface is generated from company truth, which means it can be regenerated when the workflow changes. The dashboard is a projection of the harness, not another place to store the company.
where the planes fit
No single framework needs to own the whole company.
These are design assignments, not sourced facts. Each plane owns one question and nothing else.
Control plane: goals, budgets, approvals, work status, ownership, and audit.
Runtime plane: worker identity, execution environment, task state, and events.
Composition plane: DeepSeek Harness assembles context, tools, skills, routes, policy, sessions, and artifacts.
Compiler: Company Foundry turns the portable company specification into the files each plane needs.

The DeepSeek Harness target receives presets, plugins, skill files, policy, evaluations, and profile patches. The other planes receive the goals, budgets, roles, approvals, tasks, and audit records they own.
A new harness receives an implementation specification instead of being forced into a fake integration.
The company should not be trapped in a user interface. That is the whole point.
build the smallest company before you build the company
The first release should not create departments, autonomous executives, or dozens of skills.
Build one closed loop.
Make that loop work end to end.
The first loop must prove five things:
The brief came from a real company description.
The source list contains approved data.
The artifact is useful enough to support a decision.
The review finds real issues and the route is logged.
The dashboard shows actual state rather than imagined activity.
expand only after proof
Then add the next loop: decision brief to product specification, followed by specification to isolated code plan and reviewed pull request.
Each loop adds a skill, artifact type, authority boundary, and evaluation only when the company needs it.
This keeps the system flexible because it keeps it small.
one company, several workers
The six prompts above can run in one Kimi K3 session while the first company is small.
Once the loop is stable, the same files can drive a swarm.
Company Foundry opens the packet, DeepSeek Harness assembles capabilities, the router selects each worker, and every worker writes to the same artifact contract.
You can also package a specialist worker around another model. A Claude-based coding worker can receive one repository packet, one code skill, an isolated work scope, and a required test artifact.
The useful part of the Grokbot pattern is the packaged worker with its own tool loop. The company layer still owns its memory, permissions, budget, and handoff.
prompt 07: create a specialist without creating a fake employee
That gives you the useful version of an agent swarm. The workers can differ. The company method does not.
Run it in this order:
Compile the company brief.
Generate the DeepSeek Harness capabilities.
Write one skill and its evaluation.
Run one packet with one worker.
Add parallel workers only where the artifacts can be merged safely.
Generate the Company Room from the run ledger.
Promote a result only through a written review gate.
The first milestone is not an autonomous company. It is one reviewable loop that can change workers without losing its memory.
the asset that survives
An AI-native company is not a company with the most agents. It is a company whose work can move through models and tools without losing purpose, evidence, authority, or memory.
But the company should own the thing underneath all of them.
the real asset is not the agent.
it is the method the company can run again tomorrow.
Conclusion: this has been inspired by Deepseek Harness and the everything is a plugin thesis. Edited using Kimi K3 and written by Typeless.

```text
Run this customer-research packet as a temporary four-worker swarm.

1. Coordinator: create the source plan and assign source IDs.
2. Collectors: inspect approved source groups in parallel and write evidence rows only.
3. Synthesizer: read the evidence ledger, never the collector chats, and draft the claim table.
4. Reviewer: reject every material claim without a valid source ID.

Shared rules:
- authority is observe and prepare only
- no worker may contact a customer or change a company system
- every output is written under `runs/[run-id]/`
- workers communicate through artifacts, not private summaries
- disagreements remain visible in `open-questions.yml`
- stop when the approved source list is exhausted

Return the swarm plan before starting work.
```

```text
Build the first Company Room from the schemas in `company/`.

The screen must show one real run:
- packet and owner
- approved context and source count
- selected skill version and model route
- current authority level
- swarm workers and their artifact status
- evidence gaps and failed evaluations
- cost receipt
- artifact preview
- approve, revise, and reject actions

Read state from the run ledger. Do not parse chat transcripts.
Do not invent agent activity, costs, or progress.
Every visible value must link back to a record or artifact.

Generate the app, seed it with one fixture run, and add tests for
loading, empty, failed, waiting-for-approval, and completed states.
```

```text
Read the skill registry and create `company/model-routing.yml`.

For each skill, declare:
- required capabilities
- maximum latency and cost policy
- economy, fast, and capable eligibility
- primary route and fallback route
- escalation conditions
- evaluation set used to approve a model for the lane

Place Kimi K3 in a lane only when the task requirements and evaluation justify it.
Create five representative test packets and a route receipt for each.

The receipt must record the candidates, exclusions, selected route,
reason, fallback, measured outcome, and final cost.
Do not route by model reputation or worker preference.
```

It is not an executive and it does not own company memory.
It accepts one approved work packet and receives only:

- the artifact and evaluation contracts

It must produce a plan, isolated change, test evidence, route receipt,
and handoff record. It cannot merge, deploy, message users, or expand scope.

Make the runtime model configurable so the same preset can use Kimi K3,
a Claude model, or another eligible route without changing the company contract.
Define the DeepSeek Harness preset, events, stop conditions, and tests.
